The relationship between canopy height and tree density can differ among
forest types or management histories. The same increase in canopy height
may also correspond to different changes in species composition. We extend
the [stratum-intercept example](stratum-effects-plot-sampling.html) to let
both intercepts and canopy-height slopes vary among strata, in magnitude
and species allocation.

We generate a new population, fit the model, and compare the combined
coefficients and resulting relationships with truth. We then use the familiar
prediction and aggregation steps to estimate forest species-by-DBH densities.
The DBH allocation regressions remain shared across strata.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}

## Read the prepared locations

We use the same three groups of stands and standardized canopy-height
predictor `x` as in the stratum-intercept article. The prepared table includes
both sampled plots and prediction units, identified by `dataset`. Units
crossing stratum boundaries have already been divided into portions, each
with its own area, `plot_id`, and `stratum_id`. The previous article maps
these strata and explains the preparation.

```{r}
#| label: slope-data
```

## Add stratum-specific slopes

### Magnitude

For unit $i$ in stratum $g(i)$, expected density $M_i$ and total count $N_i$
follow

$$
\log M_i=(\beta_0+\delta_{0,g(i)})+
          (\beta_1+\delta_{1,g(i)})x_i,
\qquad
N_i\mid M_i,r_M\sim\operatorname{NB}(a_iM_i,r_M),
$$

where $a_i$ is the unit's area in hectares and $r_M$ is negative-binomial
size. The stratum deviations have independent Normal distributions

$$
\delta_{0,g}\sim\operatorname{N}(0,\sigma_{\delta,0}^2),
\qquad
\delta_{1,g}\sim\operatorname{N}(0,\sigma_{\delta,1}^2).
$$

The combined intercept $\beta_0+\delta_{0,g}$ gives log expected density
at average plot canopy height. The combined slope $\beta_1+\delta_{1,g}$
describes how that log density changes with `x`. A one-standard-deviation
increase in canopy height multiplies expected density by
$\exp(\beta_1+\delta_{1,g})$. A positive slope increases expected density;
a negative slope decreases it.

### Species allocation

Species allocation again proceeds through pine, then oak, with birch
receiving the remaining trees. For allocation step $j$, we use

$$
\pi_{ij}=\Phi\left\{
  (\alpha_{0j}+\gamma_{j,0}u_{0,g(i)})+
  (\alpha_{1j}+\gamma_{j,1}u_{1,g(i)})x_i
\right\},
$$

where $u_{0,g}$ and $u_{1,g}$ are independent standard Normal scores.
Each stratum has an intercept score and a slope score, each shared by the
pine and oak allocation steps. Their species-specific loadings determine
the size and direction of each contribution. Pine anchors both terms,
so its intercept and slope loadings are constrained to be positive.
The combined slopes can still have either sign.

The two terms have separate scores and loadings. As in the magnitude model,
we model intercept and slope deviations independently; this specification
does not estimate an intercept–slope covariance. A slope changes the probit
allocation relationship, not the species probability by a constant amount.
For oak, allocation remains conditional on a tree not being pine.

## Generate a population

We keep $\beta_0=\log(350)$ and $\beta_1=-0.2$, and use magnitude
standard deviations of 0.5 for intercepts and 0.2 for slopes. Species
regression coefficients match the preceding articles. We use loadings
of 0.7 and $-0.5$ for the species intercept term and 0.4 and $-0.3$ for
the slope term. Size is fixed at 1,000 because magnitude contains random effects.

We draw the four sets of effects once per stratum and use them at all
observed and prediction units in that stratum. The `true_coefficients`
table records the resulting combined intercepts and slopes for comparison
after fitting.

```{r}
#| label: slope-effects
```

the three realized deviations need not average to zero. We use their sums
with the regression coefficients to generate total counts and species allocations.

## Fit the model

We arrange the counts into one row per unit, species, and DBH class.

```{r}
#| label: model-data

library(magComp)

species_order <- c("pine", "oak", "birch")

trees <- plots |>
  select(plot_id, stratum_id, area, x, contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(contains(":"), names_to = c("species", "dbh_class"),
               names_sep = ":", values_to = "count") |>
  mutate(
    species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
    dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes)
  ) |>
  arrange(plot_id, species, dbh_class)

dat <- magCompData(
  trees,
  unit = plot_id, categories = c(species, dbh_class),
  tree_count = count, design = fixedArea(area)
)
```

The new formula terms are `x:iid(...)` for magnitude and
`x:factor_iid(...)` for species allocation. The `x:` prefix multiplies the
term's contribution by canopy height, making it a varying slope.
Including `x` separately supplies the fixed slope. Distinct term names
identify the intercept and slope parameters in the fitted object.

```{r}
#| label: fit

fit <- magComp(
  dat,
  magnitude = ~ x + iid(stratum_id, name = "stratum_intercept") +
    x:iid(stratum_id, name = "stratum_slope"),
  composition = magCompComposition(
    species ~ x +
      factor_iid(stratum_id, K = 1, anchors = "pine", name = "stratum_intercept") +
      x:factor_iid(stratum_id, K = 1, anchors = "pine", name = "stratum_slope"),
    dbh_class | species ~ x
  ),
  control = magCompControl(
    n_samples = 4000,
    n_burn = 1000,
    n_chains = 3,
    n_cores = 3,
    chain_seeds = 1:3,
    nb_size = 1000,
    verbose = FALSE
  )
)
```

Each chain contributes 3,000 retained draws. We use automatic starting
values and default priors. The model estimates a separate magnitude
variance for each term and separate species loadings for the intercept
and slope factors. Only three strata inform these between-stratum
distributions, so we focus on the combined coefficients and their relationships.

## Inspect the combined intercepts and slopes

We first inspect the fixed regression coefficients from `summary(fit)`.
The complete summary also includes the magnitude variances, species loadings,
and DBH coefficients.

```{r}
#| label: separate-coefficients

parameter_summary <- summary(fit)

parameter_summary |>
  filter(parameter == "coefficients",
          component == "magnitude" | block == "species") |>
  select(symbol, mean, q2_5, q97_5, rhat, ess) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               col.names = c("Parameter", "Mean", "2.5%", "97.5%", "R-hat", "ESS"))
```

Several fixed coefficients mix slowly, with R-hats up to about 1.24.
As in the intercept-only extension, a fixed coefficient and its random
deviations can trade off while leaving their sums nearly unchanged.
This applies to slopes as well as intercepts. The data inform a stratum's
combined slope more directly than its fixed and random parts separately.

We obtain the combined coefficients for each stratum with the same
`summary()` interface. For magnitude, it adds the corresponding random
coefficient. For species, it adds the matching loading-times-score contribution.
These operations happen within each retained draw and chain.

```{r}
#| label: combined-coefficients

combined_summary <- summary(fit, type = "combined", group = "stratum_id") |>
  mutate(
    component = if_else(component == "magnitude", "Magnitude", str_to_title(stick)),
    stratum_id = as.integer(group)
  ) |>
  left_join(true_coefficients, by = c("component", "coefficient", "stratum_id")) |>
  mutate(
    component = factor(component, levels = c("Magnitude", "Pine", "Oak")),
    coefficient = factor(coefficient, levels = c("(Intercept)", "x"),
                          labels = c("Intercept", "Slope"))
  )

combined_summary |>
  group_by(component, coefficient) |>
  summarise(max_rhat = max(rhat), min_ess = min(ess), .groups = "drop") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3,
               col.names = c("Component", "Coefficient", "Largest R-hat", "Smallest ESS"))
```

The table summarizes diagnostics across the three strata for each coefficient.
All combined coefficients have R-hats below 1.01, with effective sample
sizes above 300. These diagnostics apply to the sums, not their separate
fixed effects, random effects, or loadings.

We compare the combined coefficients with truth. Magnitude coefficients
are on the log-density scale; species coefficients are on the probit scale.

```{r}
#| label: fig-combined-coefficients
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "True and estimated stratum-specific intercepts and slopes. Blue points and bars show posterior means and 95% credible intervals; black marks show generating values. Panels use the appropriate coefficient scale."

ggplot(combined_summary, aes(factor(stratum_id), mean)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), width = 0.15, color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(aes(shape = "Estimate"), color = "#0072B2", size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(aes(y = truth, shape = "Truth"), size = 6) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Truth" = 95, "Estimate" = 16),
                     breaks = c("Truth", "Estimate"), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(vars(component, coefficient), ncol = 2, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Stratum", y = "Combined coefficient") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The magnitude slope is positive in stratum 1 and negative in strata 2 and 3.
Pine allocation increases with canopy height in all three strata, most
strongly in stratum 2. Oak's conditional allocation slopes are negative.
We next translate these coefficients into density and species-probability
relationships, including uncertainty.

## Plot the canopy-height relationships

We construct 50 canopy-height values within each stratum's observed range.
Here `plot_id` labels evaluation points along these relationships. They
do not represent the forest prediction grid.

```{r}
#| label: relationship-data

relationship_data <- plots |>
  group_by(stratum_id) |>
  summarise(x = list(seq(min(x), max(x), length.out = 50)), .groups = "drop") |>
  unnest(x) |>
  mutate(plot_id = row_number())

relationship_draws <- predict(
  fit,
  relationship_data,
  type = c("magnitude", "proportion"),
  target = "expected",
  n_draws = 100,
  summary = "samples"
)
```

The expected target shows uncertainty in the modeled relationships. It
transforms each draw of the combined coefficients before calculating means
and intervals. We use the observation target later for forest estimation,
where predictive draws also include count and allocation variation.

### Expected tree density

We calculate the true relationships using the generating stratum effects,
then join the magnitude summaries to the evaluation points.

```{r}
#| label: magnitude-relationships

relationship_truth <- relationship_data |>
  left_join(stratum_effects, by = "stratum_id") |>
  mutate(
    magnitude = exp(beta_0 + delta_0 + (beta_1 + delta_1) * x),
    pi_pine = pnorm(alpha_pine[1] + gamma_pine[1] * u_0 +
                     (alpha_pine[2] + gamma_pine[2] * u_1) * x),
    pi_oak = pnorm(alpha_oak[1] + gamma_oak[1] * u_0 +
                    (alpha_oak[2] + gamma_oak[2] * u_1) * x),
    pine = pi_pine,
    oak = (1 - pi_pine) * pi_oak,
    birch = (1 - pi_pine) * (1 - pi_oak)
  )

magnitude_relationships <- summary(relationship_draws) |>
  filter(quantity == "magnitude") |>
  mutate(plot_id = as.integer(unit)) |>
  left_join(select(relationship_truth, plot_id, stratum_id, x, truth = magnitude),
             by = "plot_id") |>
  mutate(stratum = paste("Stratum", stratum_id))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-magnitude-relationships
#| fig-cap: "Expected tree density versus standardized canopy height by stratum. Blue lines and bands show posterior means and pointwise 95% credible intervals; dashed black lines show the true relationships."

ggplot(magnitude_relationships, aes(x, mean)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = "Estimate"), color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_line(aes(y = truth, linetype = "Truth")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Truth" = "dashed", "Estimate" = "solid"),
                        breaks = c("Truth", "Estimate"), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ stratum, nrow = 1, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "Standardized canopy height", y = "Expected density (trees/ha)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

The varying slopes capture different directions and strengths of association.
Although each relationship is linear on the log-density scale, exponentiation
gives the curved relationships on the density scale shown here.

### Species probabilities

The model returns probabilities for the 15 species-by-DBH categories. We
sum the five DBH probabilities within each species in every draw, then
summarize those species probabilities. Summing interval endpoints would
not give intervals for these sums.

```{r}
#| label: species-relationships

species_relationships <- list()

for (s in species_order) {
  categories <- paste(s, dbh_classes, sep = ":")

  # Sum DBH classes, keeping evaluation points, draws, and chains.
  proportion_draws <- apply(
    relationship_draws$proportion[, categories, , , drop = FALSE],
    c(1, 3, 4), sum
  )

  # Summarize all draws and chains at each evaluation point.
  species_relationships[[s]] <- tibble(
    plot_id = as.integer(dimnames(proportion_draws)[[1]]),
    species = s,
    mean = apply(proportion_draws, 1, mean),
    q2_5 = apply(proportion_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025),
    q97_5 = apply(proportion_draws, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975)
  )
}

species_truth <- relationship_truth |>
  select(plot_id, stratum_id, x, all_of(species_order)) |>
  pivot_longer(all_of(species_order), names_to = "species", values_to = "truth")

species_relationships <- bind_rows(species_relationships) |>
  left_join(species_truth, by = c("plot_id", "species")) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
         stratum = paste("Stratum", stratum_id))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-species-relationships
#| fig-height: 7
#| fig-cap: "Species probabilities versus standardized canopy height by stratum. Blue lines and bands show posterior means and pointwise 95% credible intervals; dashed black lines show truth. These probabilities sum to one across species at each canopy height."

ggplot(species_relationships, aes(x, mean)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(aes(linetype = "Estimate"), color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_line(aes(y = truth, linetype = "Truth")) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("Truth" = "dashed", "Estimate" = "solid"),
                        breaks = c("Truth", "Estimate"), name = NULL) +
  facet_grid(species ~ stratum, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, 1)) +
  labs(x = "Standardized canopy height", y = "Species probability") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Oak's probability includes both its conditional allocation and the chance
that a tree was not assigned to pine. Birch receives what remains, so its
relationship can be curved even without a separate regression coefficient.

## Estimate forest densities

We now predict counts and allocations over the actual forest prediction
units. The stratum intercepts and slopes are included automatically.
`standSummary()` weights the resulting densities by the represented areas,
as in the preceding articles.

```{r}
#| label: forest-predictions

set.seed(1)

predictions <- predict(
  fit,
  prediction |> select(plot_id, stratum_id, x, area),
  type = "density",
  target = "observation",
  n_draws = 100,
  summary = "samples"
)

forest_predictions <- standSummary(
  predictions,
  data = prediction,
  unit = plot_id,
  represented_area = area,
  summary = "samples"
)

forest_truth <- prediction |>
  select(contains(":")) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "category", values_to = "count") |>
  group_by(category) |>
  summarise(truth = sum(count) / sum(prediction$area), .groups = "drop")

forest_comparison <- summary(forest_predictions) |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(forest_truth, by = "category") |>
  separate_wider_delim(category, delim = ":", names = c("species", "dbh_class")) |>
  mutate(species = factor(species, levels = species_order),
         dbh_class = ordered(dbh_class, levels = dbh_classes))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-forest-densities
#| fig-cap: "Forest species-by-DBH densities. Blue points and bars show posterior predictive means and 95% intervals; black marks show the simulated forest truth."

ggplot(forest_comparison, aes(dbh_class, mean)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), width = 0.15, color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_point(aes(shape = "Estimate"), color = "#0072B2", size = 2.5) +
  geom_point(aes(y = truth, shape = "Truth"), size = 6) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("Truth" = 95, "Estimate" = 16),
                     breaks = c("Truth", "Estimate"), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~ species, nrow = 1) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(x = "DBH class (cm)", y = "Trees per hectare") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Forest estimates combine the stratum-specific relationships with the
canopy heights and areas across the forest. The same predictive draws can
be summarized by stratum or stand using the area tables and calls shown
in the [stratum-intercept article](stratum-effects-plot-sampling.html#summarize-predictions-by-stratum).

The same `x:` construction applies to spatial random effects. Use
`x:nngp(...)` for magnitude and `x:factor_nngp(...)` for species allocation,
with coordinates and neighbors specified as in the
[spatial-effects article](spatial-effects-plot-sampling.html). The canopy-height
slopes then vary continuously across the forest rather than being shared
within strata. Combined-coefficient summaries, prediction, and area aggregation
follow the same approach.

Random effects in DBH allocation within species are developed separately in the
[conditional DBH-effects article](conditional-dbh-effects-plot-sampling.html).
